Isaac: Erm, I think I did alright? I don't know, the last couple I was kind of guessing. Did you finish it?

Haider: A spreadsheet, that's organised. You're more organised than my whole office.

=== CALL C0055 ===
Tomasz: Hello. Good afternoon. Can you see me?
Darren: Yeah, I can see you, mate. Darren. You alright?
Tomasz: I am Tomasz. Yes, I am fine, thank you. Not too bad.
Darren: Where's that to then, where are you?
Tomasz: Sorry?
Darren: Sorry, where are you based, like?
Tomasz: Ah. Crawley, in West Sussex. Near Gatwick. And you?
Darren: Bridgwater, Somerset. Down the M5. Bit quieter than Gatwick, I reckon.
Tomasz: Yes, the planes are noisy when the wind changes. You get used to it. Mostly.
Darren: Ha. I had that puzzle thing at the start, did you do that? Proper did my head in, that did.
Tomasz: Yes. I finished most of them. The last one I am not sure if it was correct.

Tomasz: Er, at the moment I am not working. I was a civil engineer, drainage and highways design, for a consultancy near Gatwick. They made a restructure in the beginning of last year and I was made redundant. So now I am applying for jobs.
Darren: Oh, sorry to hear that, mate. That's rough.
Tomasz: It is okay. The company had to cut, somebody had to go. I keep a spreadsheet of every application, so I am, how do you say, organised about it at least.
Darren: More organised than me, I'll tell you that. I do cleaning, part-time, at a supermarket. Three early shifts a week. Up at half four, so I'm knackered by about two o'clock. I used to do warehouse stuff, forklift and that, but my back and my knee put a stop to it, sort of thing.

Darren: Yeah? I walk the dog along the river, the Parrett. Tyson, he's a Staffie, getting on a bit now, so it's more of a stroll than a walk, d'you know what I mean. We're both slowing down.
Tomasz: Ha. Yes. It is the same for everybody.
Darren: What's your missus do, if you don't mind me asking?
Tomasz: My wife is a senior care assistant, in a residential home.
Darren: You're joking. So's mine. Karen. Care assistant at a home, nearly full-time. Long old shifts, she does.
Tomasz: Really? That is a coincidence. Yes, it is hard work. Agnieszka comes home very tired. And the weekends also.
Darren: Proper hard. I feel a bit bad sometimes, honestly, she's doing all them hours and I'm doing my three mornings. But there you go.
Tomasz: I think you do what your body allows. It is honest work. That is what matters, I would say.
Darren: Yeah. Cheers, mate. Yeah. So what d'you do with yourself, now you're not working?
Tomasz: The garden, mainly. I have a greenhouse with tomatoes, and this year they are doing very well. And I fix things. Last week I fixed the gate of my neighbour.
Darren: Oh, you're handy then. I've got a moped in my shed I've been doing up. Six years, mind. It's nearly finished.
Tomasz: Six years. Then it must be very good when it is finished.
Darren: Ha, that's one way of putting it. Karen reckons I just go out there to get away from the telly.
Tomasz: That is also a good reason for a shed, I think.
Darren: Exactly, mate. You get it. Do you have kids?
Tomasz: Two. My son is an electrician in Horsham, and my daughter is a pharmacist in Brighton. They have left home, so it is only us now. And sometimes my daughter's cat.
Darren: Same, two grown-up. My daughter's in Bristol, she's got a little one, so I'm a grandad now. That's her in the photo behind me, actually.
Tomasz: Ah, yes, I saw the photo. Congratulations. That is—

Isaac: Ha, true. Did you do the puzzle thing at the start? I was just saying to the last guy, I always get tense with timed stuff.

Isaac: Second's still good, though.
Daniel: Second's the first loser, mate. That's what I tell my department.
Isaac: Ha. Bit harsh.
Daniel: I'm joking. Mostly. Who'd you have before me, then?

Tomasz: Three students is good. To explain something to another person, it is a real skill. I did this with the junior engineers. Some of them, I explained the same thing five times.
Isaac: Five times? And you didn't get annoyed?
Tomasz: No. The fifth time, usually they understand. And then they explain it to the next one.
Isaac: That's nice, actually. I'll remember that when my Year 11 kid asks about supply and demand again.
Tomasz: May I ask, you have the trainers in boxes in your photo. You collect them?
Isaac: Kind of. I buy limited ones and sell them on. Some I keep. The boxes keep them clean, otherwise they lose value.
Tomasz: Very sensible. Like an engineer. You protect the asset.
Isaac: Ha, protect the asset. I'm gonna tell my dad that, he thinks it's a waste of shelf space.
Tomasz: Fathers always think this. My son had a motorbike magazine collection. I said the same.
Isaac: Ha. Erm, I saw the crucifix behind you as well. Are you, like, a churchgoer?
Tomasz: Yes, Catholic. The Polish Mass, most Sundays. And you?
Isaac: Methodist, sort of. My mum goes every week. I go Christmas, Easter, when my nan's down. You kind of remind me of some of the uncles at our church, actually. In a good way, I mean.
Tomasz: Ha. I will take this as a compliment.
Isaac: It is, it is. They're the ones who always ask how uni's going and actually listen. My granddad's been ill recently, so they've been, erm, really good with the family, to be fair.
Tomasz: I am sorry about your grandfather. I hope he gets better. A church family, it helps in these times.
Isaac: Yeah. Thanks. It does, yeah.
Tomasz: And your studies, the economics. What will you do when you finish, if the bank—

C0059.line_text: Isaac: Nah, that sounds actually sick. I'd go to that. I'm kind of into, like, big events and buildings and stuff, I take a lot of photos.
C0059.what: The bedroom door behind Isaac opens and a teenage girl (his sister) leans in, unplugs a phone charger from the socket by his shelf, and leaves again; Isaac's eyes flick sideways towards her for a second while he keeps talking.
